Prabowo once again advocated for a two-state solution to end the long ongoing conflict in Gaza in front of French president Emmanuel Macron,[288] who some time before meeting Prabowo has announced plans for French recognition of Palestine.[289] He also said that he is open to normalise relations with Israel once Palestinian independence is acknowledged.[290] In his statement, Palestine's independence is the only solution for a long lasting peace in the Middle East while stating that Israel also has an inalienable right to exist as a sovereign state and Indonesia will recognise Israel only after Palestine is fully independent.[291] Despite the idea of recognising Israel after Palestine became independent became controversial, the Indonesian Ulema Council (MUI) endorsed the idea, reminding the public that his statement is not a pro-Israel statement.[292] However, MUI told that Prabowo must hold Israel accountable for their war crimes in Gaza even if he wishes to normalise ties with Israel.[292] The Prosperous Justice Party and the United Development Party also gave their support to Prabowo's statement but told Prabowo to focus more on Palestinian independence first,[293] while PDI-P politician Djarot Saiful Hidayat state that Prabowo should not rush to recognise Israel as a state, as it is considered a violation to the Constitution of Indonesia.[294]
 Prabowo at the Gaza peace summit in Sharm El Sheikh, Egypt, 13 October 2025
During the Eightieth session of the United Nations General Assembly, Prabowo reiterated his stance on recognising Israel with the condition that Israel must recognise Palestine as an independent nation.[295] While praising France, United Kingdom, Portugal and other countries for their recognition of Palestine, Prabowo also pressured those who had yet to recognise Palestine to do so as soon as possible to stop the humanitarian crisis there.[296] Once again, it sparked debate in social media with arguments for the two state solution said Prabowo's speech has placed one step closer to peace while arguments against it said that Israel's atrocities has made the two state solution no longer viable and Prabowo had violated the Constitution of Indonesia for saying in favour of Israeli recognition.[297][298] His speech generated even more controversy in social media after Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised Prabowo's speech.[299] He was nevertheless applauded domestically as Speaker Puan Maharani states her proudness as she considers Prabowo's speech as reflecting Indonesia's commitments to end the humanity crisis in Palestine,[300] while former president Joko Widodo states that Prabowo's speech is a firm and brave message for peace.[301] Internationally, US President Donald Trump was impressed especially when Prabowo pounded the podium as he spoke while French president Emmanuel Macron thanked Prabowo for his "strong" statements and told him that other countries were taking notes of his commitment.[302] Prabowo later told the media that his speech was positively received and he got words of appreciation from numerous state leaders for "truly want to find a middle path", in which he hopes to find a substantial and just way to end the conflict.[303] He later attended the Gaza Peace Summit in Sharm El Sheikh as the sole representative from Southeast Asia, witnessing the signings of the accords and offering Indonesia's support for Gaza's reconstruction while advocating for the two-state solution.[304] In his speech at the 2025 United Nations General Assembly, Prabowo remarked that Indonesia would be willing to provide up "20,000 or even more" peacekeeping personnel in case an UN mission to Gaza was authorised.[305]
India
 Prabowo with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Droupadi Murmu as chief guest of the Republic Day celebration, 2025
Prabowo was invited by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government as chief guest of the Republic Day celebration in 2025. The visit is to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries. The Indonesian president was welcomed by Minister of State for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita. The trade between the two countries in 2023 stands at USD 29.40 billion.[306] Prabowo was met by the Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar.[307] The Indian Ministry of External Affairs described the relationship as "warm and friendly… spanning over millennia." President Prabowo was given a ceremonial welcome by the President of India Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.[308] Prabowo said Indonesia considers India a great friend and the first country that recognised Indonesian independence.[309] A 352-member Indonesian military marching contingent participated in the Republic Day parade in New Delhi. During the visit the two sides are to discuss and conclude deals in trade, healthcare, digital technologies, energy and tourism, as well as the purchase of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile.[310]
Prior to his state visit to India in 2025, Prabowo claimed to have a genome test on his ancestry and the test reported him as partially Indian. In front of the Indian government, Prabowo admitted that he danced to Bollywood songs to which he attributed this habit to his DNA test result.[311] He again raised the matter when Narendra Modi visited Indonesia on 2026 and states that he cannot help himself dancing to Indian music despite in a formal setting between both leaders to which he also jokes that his ministers and generals may also have Indian DNA due to how well they sang Indian songs.[312][313]
Russia
 Prabowo and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia, 19 June 2025
On 19 June 2025, Prabowo attended the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum as a guest of honour. He met Russian President Vladimir Putin and the two heads of state signed a strategic partnership agreement. In addition, the Indonesian and Russian sovereign funds Danantara and the Russian Direct Investment Fund signed an agreement to create an investment fund worth €2 billion (US$2.9 billion).[314][315] His visit to Russia coincides with the 51st G7 summit at Kananaskis, in which Prabowo was also invited to attend but didn't.[315] Despite the apparent snub cited by Western aligned media,[316][315] Prabowo clarified his reason to skip the summit is because Indonesia's non-bloc stance and commitment issues made prior to the G7 invitation.[317][318]
Social
Free school meals (MBG in indonesia)(Makan Bergizi Gratis)
Main article: Free Nutritious Meals
His campaign team introduced a goal of a free school school lunch program by distributing free milk and lunch meals.[319] After Prabowo was declared as president-elect, pilot program of the policy was enacted. Prabowo said that he wanted to enact this because he saw nearly 25% of Indonesian children skip their breakfast and he wanted to know if the program could succeed by conducting pilot programs.[320] On 24 May 2024, he changed the program into free nutritious meal program. Overall, this program is designed with the aim of building superior resources, reducing stunting and poverty rates while driving the economy.[321] This program is also one of Prabowo's key policies in realising the Golden Indonesia 2045 Vision that targets the creation of a golden generation by utilising demographic dividends that can launch Indonesia into a developed country.[322]
The program was officially rolled out since 6 January 2025 in 26 provinces of Indonesia, carried out by the National Nutrition Agency, and targeting children from preschool to secondary school students, as well as pregnant and nursing mothers with the aim of able to bring benefit to at least 82,9 million beneficiaries.[323] However, the effectiveness of this policy was repeatedly questioned. With a huge budget needed to execute the program, the program may risk cutting the budget of other social programs and caused economic instability.[324] In addition, the program has been marked by repeated cases of food poisoning; by 15 August 2025, over 1,000 people had been sickened.[325]
People's School
Prabowo established Sekolah Rakyat, an educational initiative with the aims to break free from poverty through boarding school education. The school will be free of charge and ensure that poor families are given equal educational opportunities under a stable and conducive learning environment.[326] The program was launched on July 2025 with poor and extremely poor families as the main recipients of the program with the government has designated 53 locations across East Java, Papua, Kalimantan and East Nusa Tenggara and aimed to improve human resources quality.
Health
On 10 February 2025, Prabowo's government enacted a free health check service with aims to improve the quality of life of the population through the use of SatuSehat app launched by the Ministry of Health.[327] The government aimed to decrease mortality rate caused by disease that can be avoided through preventive healthcare such as cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes and tuberculosis.[328][329]
New capital
Construction of Nusantara under Prabowo's presidency continued despite no longer be considered as priority due to reallocation of other policies such as the free meal program.[330]
On 21 September 2025, Prabowo signed a presidential decree that officially made Nusantara as the political capital city of Indonesia and targeted for its realisation to be implemented in 2028.[331] However, this decree was met with suspicion as the decree only mandated for the House of Representatives and Regional Representative Council to move to Nusantara,[332] while analysts criticise the lack of seriousness to relocate away from Jakarta.[333]
Political views
Prabowo Subianto said in his November 2023 speech at the Institute for Development of Economics and Finance (INDEF) think thank that Indonesia needs a middle way between capitalism and socialism, which would be a Pancasila economy how the third president of Indonesia B.J. Habibie wanted.[334][335] Besides his own variant of a Third Way, he advocates for anti-neoliberalism.[336] In foreign policy, Prabowo has expressed a desire for closer diplomatic ties with China and India, while calling for distance from the West.[337] In June 2023, during his tenure as defence minister, Prabowo proposed a peace plan to end the Russo-Ukrainian War, involving holding referendums in disputed areas between the two countries, which was subsequently condemned by Ukraine for appearing pro-Russia.[338] Then-president Jokowi later clarified that Prabowo's suggestion was his personal viewpoint and did not reflect the official position of the Indonesian government.[339] In January 2022, Prabowo expressed openness to the normalisation of Indonesia–Israel relations.[340]
Controversies
Internal army dispute
In 1983, according to Sintong Panjaitan, Prabowo had a dispute with a few generals who plotted to overthrow Suharto to the point that he plotted to use Detachment 81 to attempt kidnapping these generals, including General L. B. Moerdani who was rumoured to be plotting a coup against Suharto. However, his plot was stopped by Luhut Binsar Pandjaitan, the commander of Detachment 81. Prabowo was his deputy commander at that time.[341] Major Luhut Pandjaitan ordered to cancel the attempt and confiscate all weapons and equipment. The threat of a coup against Suharto was later found to be false and Prabowo was given a leave due to stress.[342] However, Prabowo denied Sintong Panjaitan's version of the story by laughing. According to him, it was unreasonable that a captain could lead his troops to fight and kidnap a general. He calmly said that every time there was a new book, there would be a new coup accusation levelled against himself, and left everyone with their own version of the story.[342]
Prabowo was once again involved in a dispute with Moerdani ahead of the 1988 MPR General Assembly. According to Kivlan Zen, rumours persisted that Moerdani would use his office of commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to gain support from the ABRI faction to run as vice president to Suharto. Prabowo reported this to Suharto and Suharto heeded Prabowo's report by replacing Moerdani with Try Sutrisno as commander of the armed forces. The position of vice president then fell to Sudharmono.[342] Moerdani's dismissal sparked worries of a coup, however the coup never really happened. Despite this, it showed Prabowo's rising influence in the armed forces and on Suharto's decision making.[342]
Occupation of East Timor
In 1983, it was claimed that Prabowo commanded the Indonesian special forces responsible for the Kraras massacres in East Timor.[32] The survivors of these massacres were locked up in a concentration camp guarded by Prabowo's men, where many died of starvation and ill-treatment.[33] Prabowo claimed he was nowhere near the Viqueque district when the massacre happened, and neither the UN nor the government of Timor Leste have ever proffered charges of human rights violations against him.[34] José Manuel Tesoro, writing for Asiaweek in 2000, contacted four separate non-governmental organisations including Tapol in London; Solidamor in Jakarta; the HAK Foundation, headquartered in Dili; and the East Timor Action Network (ETAN) in New York, but they could not provide any eyewitness reports, transcripts of intercepted communications, leaked papers, or anything that could substantiate Prabowo's involvement.[35][32]
Kidnapping of activists
Between 1997 and 1998, Kopassus members from Team Mawar (Rose Team) were responsible for pro-democracy activists kidnappings of at least 22 people mainly in Jakarta.[343] Nine activists were released and 13 remain missing.[343][344] In 1999, 11 members of Tim Mawar were found guilty by a military court.[343] However, they appealed the verdict to the Supreme Court, which was not made public and only revealed in 2007, and were never jailed and all but one remained in the military.[343][345][346] In September 2020, Defence Minister Prabowo appointed two of the Team Mawar officers, two serving brigadier generals, to senior positions in the Ministry of Defence following approval by President Joko Widodo.[345] Amnesty International criticised the appointments as the President and the DPR had promised to investigate missing activist cases and instead placed suspects in positions of power.[343][347] and shortly after Prabowo was inaugurated as president two more members of the Team Mawar became heads of the National Cyber and Crypto Agency and the Main Secretariat of the State Intelligence Agency.[348]
Paradise Papers
See also: Paradise Papers
In November 2017, an investigation conducted by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalism cited his name in the list of politicians named in "Paradise Papers" allegations.[349]
Mirage 2000 purchase
On 13 February 2024, the Corruption Eradication Commission had received a report of alleged corruption conducted by Prabowo in the purchase of ex-Qatar Emiri Air Force Dassault Mirage 2000-5 jet aircraft which was cancelled by the Ministry of Defence due to fiscal limitations.[350][351] Allegedly, the purchased aircraft will be bought at a much higher price and there are gratification involved.[350][352] Deputy Minister of Defence Muhammad Herindra denied the allegations, dismissing the rumours as slanderous allegations and fake news.[352] In response, the Ministry of Defence appointed lawyer Hotman Paris Hutapea to lead the defence.[353] Despite being mentioned in a report that allegedly uncovered the corruption, Group of States against Corruption (GRECO) stated it had "never have done any work related to Indonesia."[354]
Political gaffes
On 18 September 2017, at the launch of a book on his father's political economy theory, Prabowo made a speech warning Indonesia could break apart in 2030. "In other countries, they have made studies, where the Republic of Indonesia has been declared no more in 2030," he said. A video clip of the speech was posted to Gerindra's official Facebook page on 18 March 2018. When asked which studies Prabowo was referring to, Gerindra official M. Husein Mohi said, "Prabowo Subianto has read various writings of people that are outside the country, intellectual observers that exist. You can also see them online."[355] It was subsequently revealed the "studies" were actually a 2015 science-fiction war novel called Ghost Fleet by US authors August Cole and P. W. Singer. A note by the authors at the start of the book states: "The following was inspired by real-world trends and technologies. But, ultimately, it is a work of fiction, not prediction."[356] Bemused by Prabowo citing the book, Singer posted on Twitter: "Indonesian opposition leader cites #GhostFleet in fiery campaign speeches... There have been many unexpected twists and turns from this book experience, but this may take the cake."[357]
In November 2018, he was embroiled in controversy for a part of his campaign in Boyolali mentioning the appearance of people in Boyolali, Central Java. After mentioning names of various luxury hotels in Jakarta whose name he claimed the rally can never pronounce, he said, "..but I am sure you have not entered these hotels. If you want to enter them you might be kicked out. You don't look like wealthy people, you have a Boyolali look." This has led to several Boyolali polling stations for 2019 election not voting him at all. Prabowo lost the regency again in 2024 election in spite of overall win in Central Java province.[358][359] The next month, Prabowo was ridiculed after erroneously stating that Haiti, a republic in the Caribbean, is an African country. In a speech made on 23 December 2018 in Solo, Central Java, Prabowo said the Indonesian government had driven part of Indonesia's wealth offshore. "If this continues to go on, Indonesia will continue to be impoverished," he said. "We, Indonesians, are on par with African impoverished countries such as Rwanda, Haiti, and small islands like Kiribati, which we don't even know where it's located," he added.[360] On 17 January 2019, in the first debate between the candidates in Indonesia's April 2019 presidential election, Prabowo said some Indonesian governors deserve higher salaries considering the size of their provinces. He gave the example of Central Java province, which he claimed is larger than Malaysia. Local media reports pointed out that Central Java is 32,544.12 square kilometres, while Malaysia is 330,323 square kilometres.[361] After the media reported on the error, Prabowo's campaign team claimed he had actually been referring to the population totals of Malaysia and Central Java.[362] In the same debate, Prabowo claimed that terrorist attacks in Indonesia were caused by poverty and perpetrated by non-Muslims disguised as Muslims, sent by other countries and controlled by foreigners. Media reports refuted his claims, pointing out that some Indonesian terrorist bombers were not poor and were not manipulated by foreigners.[363]
On 12 December 2023, Prabowo went viral after his commentary about his rival Anies Baswedan on ethics by saying "Ndasmu etik!" (English: God damn ethics!) which is considered insulting him in an internal party congress held by Gerindra. His spokesperson later stated that it was just a joke.[364] Ndasmu would appear again in Gerindra's 17th anniversary party in Bogor where Prabowo criticizes his critics over the perception that his government was a puppet government of Joko Widodo.[365]
During the anniversary of National Awakening Party on 24 July 2026, Prabowo said that there are still "londo ireng" to criticize perceived enemies of the state to which he describes them as masquerading as journalists, experts and NGOs who only seek to report on the bad results of his government policies. He said that those londo irengs still exists, just changing their clothes.[366] The Association of Indonesian Journalists (AJI) and several other NGOs demanded his apology and criticizes his speech as discrediting their profession, endangering free speech and being tone-deaf to current issues.[367] Hasan Nasbi, special advisor to the president, states that Prabowo's speech was meant to criticize troublemakers and he slammed those who demand the apology for stirring up unnecessary chaos.[368]
On 21 September 2026 in the National Mandate Party 28th anniversary party, Prabowo gave a speech criticizing experts who criticizes his free nutritious meal program, claiming that these so-called "experts" had spread lies and deceit and among these experts he said that they're, "too intelligent that (he/she) became stupid!" (Indonesian: Saking pintarnya jadi goblok).[365]
Political endorsement
During the 2024 Central Java gubernatorial election, Prabowo gave his public endorsement of support to Ahmad Luthfi and Taj Yasin Maimoen through a video uploaded in Taj Yasin's Instagram account. His endorsement was slammed by the PDI-P, and Deputy Speaker of the People's Consultative Assembly Bambang Wuryanto called the endorsement as "worrying" and reminded Prabowo that he is the president, not just a party leader.[369] Many has also questioned the ethics behind the endorsement as legal experts believed that the president of Indonesia must not meddle around with legal institutions in favour of a candidate[370] and General Election Supervisory Agency (Bawaslu) announced that they will investigate the video for any offences.[371] However, Prabowo's endorsement was also defended as NasDem politician Muhammad Rifqinizamy Karsayuda and Head of Presidential Communication Office Hasan Nasbi said that Prabowo spoke as a party chairman and there is no restrictions on presidents being a chairman of their own parties[372][373] while Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Budi Gunawan states that Prabowo's endorsement is a "normal matter" in democracies.[374] Bawaslu found that although the video featuring him did show political campaign message, their investigation result shows that he did not commit any offences because the video was posted within the social media campaign period between 25 September to 23 November, and Prabowo is allowed to campaign for his endorsed candidates as long as either he took his time off from the office or he done it on a holiday, which in Taj Yasin's clarification to Bawaslu states that the video was created on Sunday, 3 November 2024.[375]
Allegations of authoritarianism
As a president elected in 2024 and being Suharto's son-in-law, Prabowo's leadership style was criticised for his authoritarian style of rule and allegedly revived the practice of Dwifungsi, where active military personnel can concurrently serve in the civilian government while maintaining military command. His background as a military commander rises when Dwifungsi was at its peak of power. The Reformasi that has sought to limit the influence of the military in civilian government has its values now threatened by moves to again empower the military, such as the revision of the Law No. 34 Year 2004.[376]
During his time as defence minister under Joko Widodo, Prabowo is considered to have restored the role of the military in many aspects of civilian life. He was known to involve the military in government programs such as the free meal program, food estate, and many other roles that is supposed to be done by the civilian sector. Few of his cabinet ministers also have military roles, which further strengthens the perception that the direction of government tends to revive New Order-style practices.[376] His most controversial appointment in his cabinet however is when he appointed Teddy Indra Wijaya who was still active in the military to be his cabinet secretary, which generate criticism from academicians and legal experts saying Prabowo has violated the Law No. 34 Year 2004 Article 47 which states that active service members of the Indonesian National Armed Forces must resign or retire from military life if appointed or given a civilian role.[377][378][379]
Personal life
 Prabowo (centre left) at his wedding to Titiek Suharto, 1983
Prabowo married Titiek Suharto on 8 May 1983. Titiek is the daughter of Indonesian President Suharto, but the couple separated shortly after Suharto's presidency ended in 1998.[380] Prabowo saw himself as a potential successor to Suharto and remained a strong supporter of the regime.[5] Prabowo and Titiek have one son together, fashion designer Ragowo Hediprasetyo (Didit), who was born in March 1984.[381]
Prabowo is a cat lover and owns a cat named Bobby Kertanegara. Bobby was a stray who was adopted by Prabowo from the streets after a chance meeting, and he often showed up in meetings that Prabowo attended in his residence at Kertanegara.[382] It was revealed later in a small talk with Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner that he has 8 cats.[383] Aside from cats, he also owns 18 horses in his hill estate in Jonggol Mountains, Bojong Koneng, Bogor Regency (southeast of Sentul City), and he often invited guests to ride one of his horses, especially when Jokowi and Gibran visited.[384] He had once brought his horse to campaign rallies especially in Gelora Bung Karno Stadium.[385] Because of his hobby of raising horses, Prabowo is known to support equestrian sports as the Equestrian Association of Indonesia once received 28 horses from Prabowo's personal wealth to support the national team in preparation for the 2025 SEA Games while being given a medal target for polo directly from the president.[386] In a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Prabowo expressed that he dreamed to become a Mountie during his youth.[387]
Prabowo usually wears khaki clothes with many pockets. He himself stated that he liked this suit for practical reasons. Prabowo started wearing it frequently when he was paired with Megawati in the 2009 presidential election.[388]
In addition to Indonesian, Prabowo speaks the Banyumasan dialect of Javanese, his father's mother tongue,[389] and is fluent in English, Dutch, French, and German. He also has limited proficiency in Arabic, which he learned during his time in Jordan.[390]
Religion
In an interview in 2018, Prabowo stated that he was a Muslim who adhered to nationalist views.[391] He added that he had insufficient knowledge about Islam.[391] Prabowo has stated that he could not read the Quran fluently.[392]
Prabowo said that he was not born into a family steeped in Islamic teachings but grew up with his colleagues who were members of various Islamic community organisations.[393]
On 13 May 2023, Prabowo stated that he was proud to adhere to Islam, which he considers to be the pioneer in many scientific and technological breakthroughs around the world.[394] On 19 November, he stated that he felt comfortable with adhering to Islamic beliefs from the teachings of Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) because he believed that the latter advocated for a form of Islam that is tolerant, protective of society, and moderate.[395]
Health
On 30 June 2024, Prabowo announced that he was undergoing a surgery on his left foot via his Instagram account.[396] In his post, he explained that he had injured his left foot twice.[396] He first injured it when he was participating in a paratrooping exercise in West Germany while he was training with GSG 9. Additionally, he experienced another foot injury when he fell down from a cliff in a combat zone in the 1980s.[397] Prabowo, who was 30 at the time of the accident, did not experience further issues until his 2024 campaign, when he was seen walking on a limp on his left foot. This prompted rival supporters to mock his physique.[398] Prabowo underwent a successful surgery on his left foot a week later at the National Defence Central Hospital.[399][400]

The presentation of the traditional title which was accompanied by the Rambu Solo' mourning ceremony was witnessed by the Governor of South Sulawesi Syahrul Yasin Limpo, Deputy Governor of South Sulawesi Agus Arifin Nu'mang, Commander of Kodam VII/Wirabuana Major General Muhammad Nizam, Regent of Tanah Toraja Theofilus Allorerung, Regent of North Toraja Frederik Batti Sorring, along with thousands of local residents.[423]
He also received the title of Friend of Indonesian Santri from the Zainul Hasan Genggong Islamic Boarding School, Probolinggo, on 2 January 2024.[424]
On 28 February 2024, Prabowo was awarded an honorary four-star general rank by President Joko Widodo.[425]
In November 2024, Ukrposhta, Ukraine's national postal service, issued a limited-edition stamp honouring Prabowo. The initiative was spearheaded by the Ukrainian Initiative, an NGO led by Indonesianist Yurii Kosenko, who described the stamp as both a tribute to Prabowo and a symbol of Indonesia-Ukraine friendship.[426]

Indonesia,[a] officially the Republic of Indonesia,[b] is a country in Southeast Asia and Oceania, between the Indian and Pacific oceans. Comprising between 13,000 and 17,000 islands—including Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, and parts of Borneo and New Guinea—it is the world's largest archipelagic state and the 14th-largest country by area. Indonesia has extensive tropical forests and marine ecosystems that support some of the world's highest levels of biodiversity.
The Indonesian archipelago has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with evidence of early human presence including fossils of Homo erectus and Homo sapiens, and megalithic sites. By the first millennium BCE, it had become connected to regional and international maritime trade networks. Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms developed by the early centuries CE, followed by the spread of Islam and the growth of Islamic states from the late medieval period. European powers later competed to monopolise trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku during the Age of Discovery. Dutch commercial and colonial control expanded from the 17th century and extended over most of the archipelago by the early 20th century, before Indonesia proclaimed its independence in the aftermath of World War II.
Since independence, Indonesia has experienced separatist conflicts, corruption, political upheaval and natural disasters, alongside democratisation and rapid economic growth. The country today is a presidential republic with an elected legislature and consists of 38 provinces, some of which enjoy greater autonomy than others. Home to over 290 million people, Indonesia ranks fourth in the world by population and has the largest Muslim population of any country. More than half of Indonesians live on Java, the most heavily populated island in the world, while the capital Jakarta is the world's most populous city.
Indonesia has hundreds of ethnic groups and more than 700 languages, as well as diverse regional cultures. This diversity is reflected in the national motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, meaning "unity in diversity". Indonesian, a standardised variety of Malay, is the official and national language and serves as the country's lingua franca. Indonesia has the largest economy in Southeast Asia, with services and industry accounting for most output and economic activity concentrated on Java. Sea and air transport are the primary means of connecting the country's many islands. Indonesia is a middle power active in regional and global affairs and is a member of the United Nations, G20, the Non-Aligned Movement, ASEAN, and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
Etymology
Main article: Names of Indonesia
The name Indonesia is usually explained as a combination of India and the Greek word nesos, together meaning 'Indian islands'.[14] In 1850, George Windsor Earl, an English ethnologist, proposed the terms Indunesians and Malayunesians for the inhabitants of the "Indian Archipelago or Malay Archipelago", preferring the latter because he considered Indunesians too general. A colleague of his, James Richardson Logan adopted Indonesia as a geographical term for the Indian Archipelago.[15]
German ethnographer Adolf Bastian from the University of Berlin gave the term greater scholarly currency by using it in the title of his five-volume work Indonesia, or the Islands of the Malay Archipelago (German: Indonesien oder die Inseln des Malayischen Archipel), published between 1884 and 1894.[16] Dutch scholars nevertheless tended to use Malay Archipelago (Dutch: Maleische Archipel) or the Netherlands East Indies (Nederlandsch Oost Indië). Popular alternatives included Dutch East Indies, Indië, de Oost ("the East"), and, less often, Insulinde.[17]
After 1900, Indonesia became increasingly common in academic and public usage, and Indonesian nationalist organisations adopted it as an expression of national unity and freedom from colonial rule.[14] Among its early Indonesian promoters was Soewardi Soerjaningrat (Ki Hajar Dewantara), who established the Indonesisch Persbureau in The Hague in November 1918, a press bureau that used Indonesia in its name.[18]

The island of Java has yielded numerous hominin fossils generally attributed to Homo erectus, including the type specimen discovered by Eugène Dubois at Trinil.[20][21] Stone artefacts on Flores show that hominins had reached the island by at least 1.02 million years ago.[22] Homo sapiens had dispersed into Southeast Asia by at least 50,000 years ago.[23] In Sulawesi, narrative cave art has been dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years.[19][24] Flores also yielded remains of the small-bodied hominin Homo floresiensis.[25] Megalithic traditions later developed at different times across the archipelago, and stone monuments were used for burials and to honour or commemorate ancestors.[26]
Beginning in the third millennium BCE, Austronesian-speaking communities moved south from Taiwan through the Philippines and into the Indonesian archipelago, where related languages spread across most of the islands.[27][28] Settlement and subsistence practices varied across the islands, with communities combining fishing, hunting, gathering and cultivation.[29] From around 500 BCE, regional trading networks increasingly connected the archipelago with South and East Asia.[30] Goods, knowledge and technologies circulated through these networks, and, during the early centuries CE, some coastal communities in Borneo, Sumatra, and Java developed into trading ports.[31][32] Indian merchants and religious specialists brought Sanskrit literacy, Hindu and Buddhist practices, and models of kingship that local rulers adopted.[33][34]
Srivijaya, founded in southeastern Sumatra in the late 7th century, grew as a maritime trading polity and a centre of Buddhist learning and religious networks.[35][36] In central Java, rulers supported the construction of major Hindu and Buddhist monuments between the 8th and 10th centuries, including Borobudur and Prambanan.[37] Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late 13th century after Raden Wijaya used a Mongol expedition to defeat his rivals and then forced the Mongols to withdraw.[38] Its rulers claimed suzerainty over a wide network of ports across the archipelago, although beyond Java this authority was often exercised indirectly through tributary, ritual, and commercial relationships rather than continuous territorial control.[39]
By the late 13th century, Muslim rule had been established in northern Sumatra. Marco Polo reported that Perlak was a Muslim town during his visit in 1292, and a royal tomb at Pasai dated 1297 records a Muslim ruler there.[40][41] Samudra Pasai became an important pepper port and a major centre for Islamic learning.[42] Islam spread further through maritime trading networks, with Muslim communities becoming established at ports along Java's north coast and elsewhere in the archipelago.[43][44] Majapahit declined during the 15th century, and Demak emerged as an independent north-coast sultanate and an important centre of Javanese Islam.[45] Early conversions were associated with the Wali Sanga, the nine saints traditionally credited with the spread of Islam in Java.[46] Islamic practice there also incorporated elements of older Javanese culture.[47]
European contact and colonial rule
Main articles: Dutch East India Company in Indonesia and Dutch East Indies
 An 1835 painting of the submission of Prince Diponegoro to General De Kock at the end of the Java War in 1830
Before European arrival, spices from Maluku were already traded through Asian maritime networks in which Javanese and other regional merchants participated.[48][49] In this region, the sultanates of Ternate and Tidore emerged as regional powers during the 15th century.[50] The Portuguese captured Malacca in 1511 and reached Maluku the following year, where they sought control of the spice trade.[51] Dutch expeditions followed in the 1590s, and in 1602 competing Dutch companies were merged into the Dutch East India Company (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, VOC). Its charter authorised it to wage war, build fortresses, and conclude treaties in Asia.[52]
In the 17th century, local states continued to expand, including the Mataram Sultanate across much of Java and the Gowa Sultanate on the southern peninsula of Sulawesi, where the port of Makassar became a major trading centre.[53] In 1619, the VOC captured Jayakarta (present-day Jakarta) and renamed it Batavia. It developed as an administrative and commercial centre and attracted Chinese migrants and others from the archipelago.[54][55] Over the next two centuries, the VOC imposed monopolies to control the spice trade and expanded its influence in Java through military campaigns and intervention in local disputes.[56][57] The VOC was dissolved in 1800 after going bankrupt, and its possessions passed to the Dutch government.[58][59] During the Napoleonic Wars, British forces captured Java in 1811, but was returned to the Dutch in 1816.[60]
In the 19th century, Dutch power expanded across the archipelago and met sustained resistance in Java, Sumatra, and Aceh.[61] The Dutch established an outpost in western New Guinea in 1828 but abandoned it in 1836 and began permanent occupation only after 1898.[62] In Bali, a series of Dutch campaigns since 1846 against the independent kingdoms there culminated in 1908.[63] By the early 20th century, military campaigns and boundary agreements had established Dutch control over a territory that largely corresponded to present-day Indonesia, known then as the Netherlands Indies.[64] The colonial administration ruled several territories directly and governed others through local states whose rulers retained limited authority under Dutch supremacy.[64]
In Java, the Dutch had introduced the Cultivation System in 1830, requiring villagers to devote part of their land and labour to government-designated crops as payment for land tax.[65] Criticism of the system helped establish colonial policy as a subject of public debate in the Netherlands.[66] In 1901, the Dutch government adopted the Ethical Policy, which aimed to improve welfare in the Indies. The policy expanded vernacular schooling, irrigation, and other public services.[65][67] Western-style schooling also expanded, but it reached only a small minority of the population.[68] In 1905, the colonial government also began resettling people from Java to less densely populated islands.[69]
Emergence of Indonesia and independence
Main articles: Indonesian National Awakening and Indonesian National Revolution
 Indonesian nationalists riding through the streets, November 1945
Colonial education, despite its limited reach, helped produce an educated elite who became active in the emerging nationalist movements.[70] Several political organisations were founded during this period, including Budi Utomo and Sarekat Islam,[71] followed by the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI) and the Indonesian National Party.[72] During the 1920s, a shared national identity began to develop through youth associations and a growing body of literature in Malay, which had long been a lingua franca that did not favour any single ethnic group. Intellectuals increasingly called the language Bahasa Indonesia and made it a common medium for the emerging nation.[73] The Youth Pledge in 1928 recognised it as the "language of unity", alongside the ideals of one homeland and one nation, Indonesia.[74][75]
The Great Depression reached the colony in the early 1930s, bringing severe economic hardship and increasing fears among colonial authorities that discontent could strengthen radical nationalist movements. Restrictions on nationalist activity became stricter, and by the mid-1930s, Sukarno, Mohammad Hatta, Sutan Sjahrir, and other non-cooperative nationalist leaders had either been imprisoned or exiled.[76] In 1942, Dutch colonial rule collapsed following the Japanese conquest of the colony during the Pacific War.[77][78]
Japanese occupation imposed martial law, banned political parties and mobilised Indonesians through Japanese-sponsored civil and quasi-military organisations.[79] Wartime shortages and forced labour caused widespread hardship, but the ban on the Dutch language strengthened the public use of the Indonesian language.[80][81] Japanese-sponsored forces such as PETA and the Sumatran Giyugun trained tens of thousands of Indonesians.[82] One day after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, Japanese authorities permitted Indonesian leaders to begin preparing institutions and a constitution for an independent state planned for September 1945.[83]
However, Japan surrendered to the Allies on 15 August 1945. Two days later, Sukarno proclaimed Indonesian independence, with Hatta co-signing the declaration.[84][85] They were named president and vice-president on 18 August.[86] Dutch attempts to restore colonial rule led to a four-year military and diplomatic struggle.[87] International opposition to the Netherlands intensified after its offensive of December 1948, and the United States subsequently pressed the Dutch into negotiations recommended by the United Nations.[88] On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty to the federal United States of Indonesia, except over western New Guinea.[89][90] The federal states soon dissolved, and a unitary republic was proclaimed on 17 August 1950.[90]
Sukarno era and Suharto's New Order
Main articles: Liberal democracy period in Indonesia, Guided Democracy in Indonesia, and New Order (Indonesia)
Sukarno (left) and Suharto (right), Indonesia's first two presidents
Indonesia adopted a parliamentary system of government under the 1950 provisional constitution.[91] The early republic faced armed opposition from the Darul Islam rebellion, whose supporters aimed to establish an Islamic state.[92] In February 1958, dissidents in West Sumatra proclaimed its own government before being joined by rebels in Sulawesi. They were seeking reforms to the republic rather than separation but were defeated by the central government.[93] After the Constituent Assembly failed to secure the required majority for a permanent constitution, Sukarno dissolved it by decree in 1959 and restored the 1945 Constitution.[94]
This established Guided Democracy, a system characterised by dominant presidential authority, less regional autonomy and a reduced role for political parties.[95] Under this system, Sukarno expanded the military's political role while supporting the growing PKI as a counterweight.[91] He also promoted state enterprises and import substitution, even as foreign investment declined, inflation soared and shortages of consumer goods worsened by the mid-1960s.[96] The western New Guinea dispute culminated in the US-mediated New York Agreement in 1962, and Indonesia administered the territory in 1963.[97][98] Not long after, Sukarno pursued Konfrontasi, opposing the formation of Malaysia through diplomatic pressure and armed incursions into its territory.[99][100]
After the 30 September Movement killed six generals in 1965, forces of Major General Suharto took control of Jakarta, and the military presented the movement as an attempted coup d'etat by the PKI.[101][102] The ensuing anti-communist campaign spread across the country, with army units working alongside or directing civilian groups.[103][102] At least 500,000 people were killed over the course of a few months, and hundreds of thousands others were detained.[c][107][108] The campaign destroyed the PKI and shifted power to the military.[109] The Supersemar order in 1966 gave Suharto de facto control over key executive and security powers, an effective transfer of power from Sukarno.[110][111]
Suharto's "New Order" restricted political organisation, embedded the military in government, and used his political party Golkar and a tightly controlled party system to dominate elections.[112] The Act of Free Choice in 1969 formally incorporated western New Guinea into Indonesia, but just over a thousand selected community leaders took part in it amid reports of military intimidation.[113] Many Papuans opposed this integration and have waged an armed resistance since then.[114][115] In 1975, Indonesia invaded Portuguese Timor and annexed it the following year.[116][d] Hasan di Tiro founded the Free Aceh Movement in 1976 and declared independence from Indonesia. The insurgency in Aceh was largely suppressed by 1979 but revived in 1989 after the return of fighters trained in Libya, prompting a military campaign lasting a decade.[118]
The New Order encouraged renewed foreign investment and sought foreign aid while pursuing industrialisation through state development plans.[119] From the 1970s, the regime greatly expanded the transmigration programme, resettling families from Java to other islands.[69] Manufacturing expanded and the number of people below the official poverty line fell substantially by the mid-1990s.[120] At the same time, conglomerates connected to Suharto's family and close associates accumulated wealth through state patronage and political protection.[121][122] The Asian financial crisis of 1997–98 caused a sharp economic downturn,[123][124] followed by protests and riots in May 1998, culminating in Suharto's resignation.[125]
Reformasi and contemporary Indonesia
Main article: Reform era in Indonesia
 Damage following the earthquake and subsequent tsunami in Banda Aceh, January 2005
The post-Suharto transition was marked by communal violence, including religious conflict in Maluku and ethnic clashes in Kalimantan.[126] This period, known as Reformasi, brought constitutional amendments, competitive elections, and decentralisation.[127][128] President B. J. Habibie relaxed restrictions on the press and political parties, oversaw the 1999 general election and the independence referendum in East Timor.[129][e] Decentralisation began in 2001 under President Abdurrahman Wahid,[133] while constitutional amendments were completed in 2002 during Megawati Sukarnoputri's presidency. One of the amendments paved the way for direct presidential elections.[134]
Although the military lost its reserved parliamentary seats, their influence did not disappear.[135] Democratic institutions were established, but patronage and influence of oligarchy persisted.[136] Former general Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono won the first direct presidential election in 2004.[137] His administration reached a peace agreement with Aceh separatists in 2005 after the previous year's Indian Ocean tsunami brought more international attention to the province.[138] Sporadic bombings occurred throughout the 2000s but had declined by the early 2010s.[139]
Joko Widodo, popularly called Jokowi, was elected president in 2014 and prioritised infrastructure and economic development, which he linked to improving welfare.[140][141] Indonesia remained an electoral democracy, but the quality of its democracy declined amid weakened parliamentary opposition and oversight, curbs on dissent, reduced independence of the anti-corruption commission, and Jokowi's intervention in the 2024 election.[142][143] Under his successor Prabowo Subianto, the government pursued a fiscally expansive programme[144] and revised a military law in 2025, which allowed more active officers to serve in civilian posts.[145]
Geography
Main articles: Geography of Indonesia and List of islands of Indonesia
 A satellite image of the Indonesian archipelago Indonesia lies within one of the most tectonically active regions on Earth.[146] Pictured above is Lake Toba in North Sumatra, the world's largest known Cenozoic caldera.[147]
Indonesia is an equatorial archipelago of coastal plains, mountains, and volcanic islands. It lies between latitudes 11°S and 6°N and longitudes 95°E and 141°E.[148] The country is the world's largest archipelagic state, extending 5,120 kilometres (3,181 mi) from east to west across three time zones and 1,760 kilometres (1,094 mi) from north to south.[149] Indonesia shares land borders with Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and Malaysia, as well as maritime borders with seven other countries, including Australia, Singapore, and the Philippines.[150] Several straits in the archipelago, including Malacca, Sunda, and Lombok, are strategic shipping routes between the Indian and Pacific oceans.[151]
Indonesia's archipelagic and territorial waters cover more area than its land counterpart, with its exclusive economic zone (EEZ) extending the rights over marine resources farther offshore.[152][f] The country is recognised as an archipelagic state under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, exercising sovereignty over the waters within its archipelagic baselines, subject to the navigational rights of others.[154][g] Indonesia has designated three north–south archipelagic sea-lane systems for international navigation through the waters between its islands, while passage rights continue along other normally used routes.[156]
The number of Indonesian islands varies by counting method, with published figures ranging from 13,000 to as high as 25,000. The most widely cited official count places the total at 17,508 islands,[157] with about 6,000 of them inhabited.[158] Its five main islands are Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Borneo, and New Guinea. Indonesia occupies most of Borneo, where it is known as Kalimantan, and the western part of New Guinea, commonly called Papua. The remainder of those islands is shared with Brunei and Malaysia, and with Papua New Guinea, respectively.[158]
Java accounts for less than 7% of Indonesia's land area but is its most populous island, with intensive farming and extensive urban growth.[159] Forest cover differs considerably, with larger forested areas in Papua and Maluku than in Java and Bali.[160] At 4,884 metres (16,024 ft), Puncak Jaya on New Guinea is the highest peak,[161] while Lake Toba on Sumatra is the largest lake.[162] In Kalimantan, major waterways like the Kapuas, Barito, and Mahakam rivers have historically served as corridors for movement and trade between communities in the interior and those near the coast.[163]
Indonesia occupies a complex plate-boundary zone where the Eurasian, India-Australia, and Pacific-Philippine sea tectonic plates interact, with subduction zones along these boundaries producing frequent earthquakes and volcanic activity.[164][165] The resulting volcanic belt contains at least 127 active volcanoes.[146] This tectonic setting exposes the archipelago to major earthquake and tsunami hazards. The Sumatra earthquake in 2004 generated a tsunami that caused widespread destruction in Aceh.[166] The Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago is one of the largest known explosive eruptions in Earth's history,[147] and the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora was followed by global cooling and the Year Without a Summer in 1816.[167]
Climate
Main articles: Climate of Indonesia and Climate change in Indonesia
 Rain clouds over Indonesia during the monsoon season, observed by the Himawari-8 weather satellite in March 2020.
Indonesia's equatorial position and monsoon winds give it a tropical climate. Most lowland areas are warm and humid throughout the year, while higher terrain is cooler, and seasonal temperature differences are small.[168] Seasonal changes in the monsoon generally bring wetter conditions from November to April and drier conditions from May to October, but their timing and intensity vary by region.[168][169] Much of the country has a tropical rainforest climate, and tropical monsoon and savanna climates occur on parts of the islands.[170] Seasonal rainfall affects rice-planting schedules and the risk of droughts, floods, and fires.[171][172]
Western Sumatra, western Java, and portions of Kalimantan and Papua receive the highest annual rainfall, whereas regions in closer proximity to Australia, such as Nusa Tenggara, experience a much drier climate.[173] The surrounding oceans, island geography, monsoon winds, and topography all affect where and when rain falls.[174] In drought-prone regions of the country, El Niño can suppress rainfall and prolong dry periods, causing water shortages and crop losses.[175][176]
Indonesia already faces climate-related hazards. Climate projections indicate further warming and sea-level rise, changes in rainfall patterns, and greater risks from extreme heat and flooding.[177] These changes affect agriculture, water resources, public health, coastal settlements and wildfire management.[178] Sea-level rise is especially relevant to coastal areas, where much of the population and infrastructure are located.[179] The country is among the largest emitters of greenhouse gas emissions.[180] It has committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2060,[181] but has faced challenges because coal-fired power generation has continued to grow despite increases in renewable energy.[182]
Biodiversity and conservation
Main articles: Fauna of Indonesia, Flora of Indonesia, Environment of Indonesia, and Conservation in Indonesia
See also: List of biosphere reserves of Indonesia and List of national parks of Indonesia
 The Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) is one of Indonesia's officially designated national animals.
Indonesia is among the 17 countries identified as megadiverse by Conservation International. Its many islands and geological history have helped produce a diverse flora and fauna.[183][184] Wallacea is a transition zone between Asian and Australian fauna and one of the world's largest centres of endemism.[185] In 2015, an estimated 83% of Southeast Asia's old-growth forest was in Indonesia.[186] Mangrove forests, coral reefs and seagrass beds make up much of the coastal ecosystems.[187]
Large palm oil and timber plantations were estimated to account for more than 40% of national deforestation between 2001 and 2016.[188] Conversion of forest land for farming, roads, and other development breaks up remaining habitat, which affects species populations, habitat quality, and biodiversity.[189] Carbon-rich peatlands are vulnerable to fires after drainage, especially during droughts.[190] Forest and peatland fires produce haze that affects public health in Indonesia and neighbouring countries, including Malaysia and Singapore.[191] At sea, coral diversity has been found to be lower on polluted or anchor-damaged reefs, while coral cover has declined sharply during prolonged periods of extreme ocean heat.[192][193]
Indonesia has designated 554 protected areas covering 27 million hectares, equivalent to 14% of its land area.[194] Assessments conducted in 2015, 2017 and 2019 found improvements in management scores but identified poaching, illegal logging, human settlements, tourism and non-timber cultivation as the main threats to protected areas.[194] The country's social forestry programme seeks to recognise customary communities' rights to manage forestland, but bureaucratic barriers have hindered its implementation.[195]
Government and politics
Main article: Politics of Indonesia
See also: Government of Indonesia
 Merdeka Palace, the official residence of the President of Indonesia
Indonesia is a unitary republic with a presidential system under the 1945 Constitution.[196] Between 1999 and 2002, four constitutional amendments introduced direct presidential elections, created new state institutions, reduced the powers of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), and gave regional autonomy a constitutional basis.[197] Following the fall of Suharto in 1998, decentralisation transferred substantial lawmaking powers to provincial, regency and city governments.[198]
The president serves as head of state and government, commands the armed forces, and may serve no more than two five-year terms.[199][200] The MPR comprises elected members of the House of Representatives (DPR) and the Regional Representative Council (DPD). It can amend the constitution, inaugurate the president and vice-president, and remove them through constitutional procedures.[201] The DPR exercises legislative, budgetary and oversight powers,[202] while the DPD may propose and consider bills concerning regional affairs but has more limited authority.[203]
Indonesia's legal system follows mainly the civil-law tradition, along with customary (adat) and Islamic law in matters such as marriage and inheritance.[204] Judicial power is exercised by the Supreme Court and its subordinate courts, and the Constitutional Court.[205] The Supreme Court hears final appeals and reviews regulations below the level of statutes.[206] The Constitutional Court reviews laws for constitutionality and adjudicates disputes over state powers, political parties and election results. It also determines whether allegations against the president or vice-president meet the constitutional grounds for impeachment.[207] The Religious Courts hear cases involving marriage, divorce, inheritance and certain transactions governed by Islamic law.[208] The Judicial Commission proposes candidates for the Supreme Court and oversees judicial conduct.[209]

Since the return to competitive elections in 1999, Indonesia has had a fragmented multi-party system. No party has won a majority in legislative elections, and presidents have usually governed through broad coalitions that include many parties in the legislature and cabinet.[210]
Political parties are often distinguished by their orientation towards secular nationalism or political Islam.[h][211] Party politics often relies more on patronage and elite power-sharing, with parties forming flexible coalitions to maintain access to state resources.[212] Opposition parties have at times joined presidential power-sharing arrangements after elections.[213]
Indonesia held its first general election in 1955.[214] Direct presidential elections began in 2004.[215] General elections are held every five years, with political parties contesting DPR seats and individuals standing for the DPD.[216] National elections require large-scale logistics, because ballots and other materials must reach remote islands, mountainous areas and places with limited infrastructure.[217]
Administrative divisions
Main article: Subdivisions of Indonesia
Indonesia is divided into provinces, which are further divided into regencies and cities. Under the general system, these levels are headed by governors, regents and mayors, respectively, and have elected regional legislatures.[218] Regencies and cities are divided into districts, followed by villages (desa) or urban villages (kelurahan).[219] Villages exercise local self-government, whereas urban villages form part of the district administration.[220]
Decentralisation after 1998 gave provincial, regency and city governments greater authority over local affairs.[198] Special autonomy arrangements apply to Aceh, which may implement aspects of Islamic law, and to Papua.[221] The Special Region of Yogyakarta retains a hereditary sultan as governor,[222] while Jakarta has special provincial autonomy as the national capital.[223] In 2022, Nusantara in East Kalimantan was designated as the future national capital. Its formal transfer from Jakarta requires a presidential decree.[224]
